topic_candidates.title: Claude Just Solved a 25-Year Cryptography Mystery. Should We Trust the Method?
topic_candidates.query: Anthropic Claude ECDSA curve origins October 16 2026
topic_candidates.brief: Anthropic says Claude traced the mysterious numbers behind widely used ECDSA security curves to an old random-number generator seeded by timestamps. In plain English: an AI found the recipe behind a locked mathematical box, but it did not break the encryption protecting people’s accounts. The useful takeaway is how AI can search millions of patterns quickly—while humans still need to verify the result. Would you trust an AI discovery before experts checked every step?
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: Strongest fresh discussion signal in the supplied headlines: Hacker News ranked it at 1,034 points with 380 comments. Anthropic published the finding on October 16, 2026 and says the result makes a deliberate backdoor less likely, not more likely. Visual potential is excellent: show a locked box, a clock seed, a simple random-number machine and the AI’s pattern search. The science angle is real but explainable: pseudorandom generators, timestamps and how repeated mathematical patterns can reveal an old recipe. ([anthropic.com](https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.science_angle: How a weak old random-number generator, seeded by a clock, can leave a recognizable mathematical fingerprint.

topic_candidates.title: The AI Coding Tool Breach That Could Turn Into a Surprise Bill
topic_candidates.query: OpenCode breach API keys leaked October 17 2026
topic_candidates.brief: OpenCode warned that some third-party AI provider keys stored in its service may have been exposed after an intrusion. Those keys can act like prepaid access cards to AI accounts, so the risk is not just stolen data—it can be unauthorized model usage and unexpected charges. This gives viewers a practical question: should AI tools ever store the keys that connect them to other services?
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: Very strong rising signal: the supplied Hacker News list shows 836 points and 156 comments, while mainstream reporting says OpenCode confirmed the incident and urged users to revoke affected keys. It is broad because ordinary users increasingly connect AI tools to paid accounts, documents and work systems. Visual potential is high: animate an API key as a house key, then show how one compromised key can open several AI accounts. Evidence is good but the exact scope remains limited, so the video should clearly separate confirmed facts from user reports. ([notebookcheck.net](https://www.notebookcheck.net/OpenCode-hacked-users-urged-to-revoke-their-API-keys.1426957.0.html?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.science_angle: How authentication tokens work, why a leaked key can authorize automated spending, and why rate limits do not equal security.

topic_candidates.title: AI Passed the Tests—but Are We Testing the Jobs People Actually Do?
topic_candidates.query: Mercor benchmark map 90 percent US working hours October 16 2026
topic_candidates.brief: A new Mercor benchmark map estimates that about 90% of US working hours involve tasks with little or no coverage in today’s common AI tests. That does not mean AI fails at 90% of work; it means impressive scores may describe only a narrow slice of real jobs. The story turns a technical debate into an everyday one: can a system ace an exam and still struggle with your actual workday?
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: The supplied Hacker News headline reached 603 points and 551 comments, showing unusually strong discussion for a work-and-AI story. Mercor’s own map explains that it matched AI benchmarks against thousands of occupational tasks and estimates how much working time those tests cover. This is highly comment-friendly for students, parents, employees and small-business owners. Visual potential is excellent: contrast a neat multiple-choice test with interruptions, judgment calls, messy files and customer conversations. Evidence is strongest when phrased as Mercor’s estimate rather than an objective measurement of all AI capability. ([mercor.com](https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.science_angle: Why measuring AI requires representative tasks, not just clean test questions, and how sampling changes what a score means.
